title: London Air Quality II
text:
Use the same practice CSV and compare PM₂.₅ on Street A and Street B. The example treats each row as a separate sampling point and assumes observations are independent. For your fieldwork, decide what counts as one observation before comparing groups.

air <- read.csv("data/london-air-quality-practice.csv")
street_a <- air$pm25[air$street == "Street A"]
street_b <- air$pm25[air$street == "Street B"]

tapply(air$pm25, air$street, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

Street A Street B 
    16.5     12.5 

tapply(air$pm25, air$street, sd, na.rm = TRUE)

Street A Street B 
2.878492 2.449490 


tapply() runs the function once per street. Compare both the averages and the spread.

boxplot(pm25 ~ street, data = air, ylab = "PM2.5 (µg/m³)")

title: London Air Quality II
text:
Test the difference in means

mean(street_a, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(street_b, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 4

t.test(street_a, street_b)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  street_a and street_b
t = 2.9933, df = 13.651, p-value = 0.009907
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 1.127009 6.872991
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
     16.5      12.5 


The default is Welch’s two-sample t-test. It tests whether the two population means are equal while allowing the groups to have different variances. Report the mean difference in µg/m³ (Street A minus Street B), the 95% confidence interval and the p-value. A small p-value indicates that a test statistic this extreme would be unusual if the population means were equal and the test assumptions held.

title: London Air Quality II
section: Match the analysis to your fieldwork
text:
Match the analysis to your fieldwork

Separate points on each street. Use the two-sample approach if the observations are reasonably independent. Check for strong skew or outliers, particularly with few points.
Several readings per stop. If the target is a comparison of sampling points, summarise readings within each point first. Nearby points may still share conditions.
Matched measurements. For a genuine pairing, such as two conditions measured at each of the same stops, align by stop ID and check that each complete pair appears once before using t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE).

Field task. Compare one pollutant across two street groups using consistent units. Include sample sizes, a plot and a short interpretation. Limit your conclusion to the locations and conditions you sampled.

title: R Essentials for London Air Quality
text: This lesson is for Geography with Social Data Science students using R for the first time. You’ll practise opening a monitor export, checking what it contains and making a plot before analysing your own London street measurements.
crumbs: R Essentials for London Air Quality

title: R Essentials for London Air Quality
text:
Run your first R code
Open your working folder in Positron with File → Open Folder. Use the session picker to start or select R. Type 2 + 3 in the Console and press Enter. R prints [1] 5.
Create a text file and save it as air-quality.R. Put the code below in the script. To run it, select both lines and press Cmd+Enter on macOS or Ctrl+Enter on Windows/Linux. The Console shows the result.

readings <- c(12, 15, 18)
mean(readings)

[1] 15


c() combines three values into a vector. The arrow <- saves that vector as readings. The function mean() calculates its average. Keep your code in the script so you can rerun it later.
crumbs: R Essentials for London Air Quality

title: R Essentials for London Air Quality
text:
Import and check a CSV
The practice CSV contains simulated readings from two London street settings. Each row represents a different sampling point. pm25 and pm10 are particulate matter concentrations in µg/m³. The example assumes your monitor records both. Use the measures and units shown in your own export.
The CSV is included with the project. If you’re following the website online, download it and save it in a folder called data inside your working folder.

air <- read.csv("data/london-air-quality-practice.csv")
head(air, 3)

  site_id   street pm25 pm10
1     A01 Street A   14   28
2     A02 Street A   18   32
3     A03 Street A   12   27

str(air)

'data.frame':   16 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ site_id: chr  "A01" "A02" "A03" "A04" ...
 $ street : chr  "Street A" "Street A" "Street A" "Street A" ...
 $ pm25   : int  14 18 12 21 16 19 15 17 9 15 ...
 $ pm10   : int  28 32 27 35 29 35 34 32 20 29 ...

table(air$street)


Street A Street B 
       8        8 


head() previews the first rows. str() shows whether columns are numeric or text. table() counts rows per street. Use View(air) in Positron to open the data in the Data Explorer. If R cannot find the file, run getwd() to check where it is looking.
crumbs: R Essentials for London Air Quality

title: R Essentials for London Air Quality
text:
Select readings and summarise them

street_a <- air$pm25[air$street == "Street A"]
summary(street_a)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  12.00   14.75   16.50   16.50   18.25   21.00 

sd(street_a, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 2.878492


$ selects a column. Brackets keep the values for rows where the street label matches. summary() shows the minimum, quartiles, median, mean and maximum. The standard deviation from sd() describes spread around the mean in the original units. na.rm = TRUE leaves missing values out of that calculation. Check and report how many readings are missing when you use your own file.
crumbs: R Essentials for London Air Quality

title: R Essentials for London Air Quality
text:
Plot and compare

boxplot(pm25 ~ street, data = air, ylab = "PM2.5 (µg/m³)")








The formula pm25 ~ street tells R to plot PM₂.₅ by street. Find the plot under Plots in Positron. The line inside each box marks the median. The box spans the middle half of the readings. Which street has the higher median? How much do the groups overlap?
crumbs: R Essentials for London Air Quality

title: R Essentials for London Air Quality
text:
Before using your field data
Keep the raw export and work from a copy. Record the street, sampling point, time, pollutant and units. Check that the concentration column imported as numeric and that zero readings and missing values are distinguishable. If you took several readings at one stop, keep a point or visit identifier so you can account for repeat measurements.
Next, use London Air Quality I to explore two pollutants measured together, then London Air Quality II to compare streets.
crumbs: R Essentials for London Air Quality

title: What is RStudio (or R)?
text:
R (or RStudio) is a statistical programming package that allows users to carry out a wide range of statistical analyses. It can also function as GIS software, enabling various types of analysis on geographical data. In the same way, it can be used for data management and geoprocessing—for example, importing different types of data, whether non-spatial or spatial, and preparing them for analysis.
There are two versions:









The famous icon on the left is the version for R (Base), and the one on the right is the version for RStudio. Both software packages are the same. The only difference is that RStudio is attractive, intuitive, and more importantly, it is user-friendly than Base R. So, we will be using this version (i.e., RStudio) throughout this workshop.
Let us talk about the installation of RStudio on your personal computer.














[Watch on YouTube]
RStudio is an open-source software, it is free. It is widely recommended in data science, scientific research, and technical communication because it is easy to access, download, and install.
To use RStudio, you must first install R (Base) before installing RStudio. Follow the steps below to install both programs for your operating system (Windows or Mac).
Steps

Download the R (Base) installer from the table below, then run the file to complete the installation.
Next, download the RStudio installer from the table below, then run the file to complete the installation.

RStudio-2026.09.0-174.dmg









Important

Windows users: use the files in the first row.
Mac (Intel) users: use the files in the second row.
Mac (M1-5 chip) users: use the files in the third row.



This section covers how to download and install RStudio for it to be used locally on your machine. There are several ways to access RStudio:

Directly through UCL Workstation PC
Remotely through the UCL Desktop@Anywhere remote service with your laptop.

Let us quickly go through these options.












[Watch on YouTube]
Go to any PC cluster in UCL and simply log on to a computer. Use the UCL Applications tool to access the desired software.












[Watch on YouTube]
To use RStudio (or any other software which UCL provides as service to students) remotely from your laptop/PC/tablet, you can:

Go to https://www.ucl.ac.uk/isd/services/computers/remote-access/desktopucl-anywhere.
Click on the blue button that says: “Log in to Desktop @ UCL Anywhere.”
You will be prompted to enter your UCL username (username@ucl.ac.uk) and password. Enter the correct credentials to gain access to the remote portal.
If you see the option “Use Web Browser”, select it to run the remote functions directly in your browser without installing the Citrix Workspace application.
You should now see a Desktop @ UCL Anywhere button – click this button to complete the login. At this point, it will feel as though you are using a UCL workstation in a cluster room or library, but remotely.
On the desktop, click the UCL Applications icon and search for RStudio.
Select the latest version available (check the year) and open it with a single click (not multiple clicks).

Voilà! You now have remote access to RStudio.

title: London Air Quality I
text:
The GEOG0186 practical explores relationships using readings from London monitoring stations. Here you’ll use the same scatterplot, correlation and regression workflow with paired pollutant measurements of the sort you might collect with a handheld monitor. Practise on the simulated CSV from R Essentials, then repeat the analysis with your own field data.
Open a new R script in Positron and run these chunks from top to bottom. Start with one street so the graph addresses a relationship within that street.

air <- read.csv("data/london-air-quality-practice.csv")
one_street <- subset(air, street == "Street A")
one_street <- one_street[complete.cases(one_street[c("pm25", "pm10")]), ]
nrow(one_street)

[1] 8


complete.cases() keeps only rows with both measurements. With your field data, check how many rows were dropped and investigate why.

title: London Air Quality I
text:
The GEOG0186 practical explores relationships using readings from London monitoring stations. Here you’ll use the same scatterplot, correlation and regression workflow with paired pollutant measurements of the sort you might collect with a handheld monitor. Practise on the simulated CSV from R Essentials, then repeat the analysis with your own field data.
Open a new R script in Positron and run these chunks from top to bottom. Start with one street so the graph addresses a relationship within that street.

air <- read.csv("data/london-air-quality-practice.csv")
one_street <- subset(air, street == "Street A")
one_street <- one_street[complete.cases(one_street[c("pm25", "pm10")]), ]
nrow(one_street)

[1] 8


complete.cases() keeps only rows with both measurements. With your field data, check how many rows were dropped and investigate why.

title: London Air Quality I
text:
Draw a scatterplot

plot(
  one_street$pm25, one_street$pm10,
  xlab = "PM2.5 (µg/m³)", ylab = "PM10 (µg/m³)",
  pch = 19
)
fit <- lm(pm10 ~ pm25, data = one_street)
abline(fit, col = "#176B5B", lwd = 2)








Each dot uses two readings from the same sampling point. Before interpreting the line, look for a clear direction or a point that might strongly influence the fit.

title: London Air Quality I
text:
Describe the relationship

cor(one_street$pm25, one_street$pm10)

[1] 0.8160943

coef(fit)["pm25"]

     pm25 
0.8965517 


The first result is the Pearson correlation. It ranges from −1 to +1 and describes the direction and strength of a straight-line relationship. The second is the fitted slope. It gives the difference in fitted PM₁₀, in µg/m³, associated with a 1 µg/m³ higher PM₂.₅ reading.
PM₂.₅ is part of PM₁₀, so some association is expected. A relationship between these readings cannot by itself identify a pollution source.
Field task. Choose two measures taken at the same points and times. If your device records only one pollutant, use a numeric field variable measured alongside it, such as a traffic count. Label both axes with units and describe the pattern in one or two sentences. If your data include repeated observations at one stop, identify those repeats before drawing conclusions about differences between locations.
